name: Olga Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the supermarket depot by half four, check the 26-tonne rigid over, tyres, lights, the tail lift, then load up with cages of chilled and ambient for three or four stores. Most days it's the same run out along the ring road and back by lunch, then a second shorter one. I like the quiet first hour when the roads are empty and it's just me and the radio. What wears me out is the store yards, where nobody's ready for you and you're stood there twenty minutes with the engine off watching your time slip.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving, and how did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years now, I got my licence at twenty through a union-backed training scheme after I left a call centre I hated. My uncle drove buses and always said a licence is something nobody can take off you. I live with my partner Jonas, who fixes buses at the council garage, and we rent a flat above a dry cleaner's. I'm not one for gadgets, I don't even use the depot's app unless they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the canteen, that I told you so. Every year there's some new thing that's meant to change the job, and every year I'm still the one backing a rigid into a yard built for a horse and cart. I'd probably not post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. My job's steady, the supermarket isn't going anywhere, and the union agreement gives us a pay rise most years. The only worry is the rent, which keeps going up faster than the pay rise, but that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. Same shifts, keep paying into the union, keep putting a bit away each month, maybe a hundred a month into the savings pot so we've got more than the three months we have now. I wouldn't go near any AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent going up. What would you do if it jumped again next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas and I would look further out, past the ring road, where flats are cheaper but the drive to the depot is longer. I'd hate that, because at half four in the morning every ten minutes counts. We'd manage though, we've got some savings and two steady wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would the depot itself change at all in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the planners get a better route program, the kind that tells you which store first. That's fine with me as long as it doesn't start timing my toilet breaks. There's already a camera in the cab that beeps if I yawn, and that's as much technology as I need in my life.

say: I'd tell the canteen **I told you so** about the hype.
I'd say the job is still **backing a rigid** into tight store yards.
think: My job feels **steady**, with a union pay rise most years.
The real pressure is **rent** climbing faster than my pay, not AI.
do: Keep the **same shifts** at the supermarket depot and stay in the union.
Save about **a hundred a month** to stretch the three-month cushion.
Avoid **AI tools** completely unless the depot makes them compulsory.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a little smugness that the hype came to nothing.
S0.quote: There's already a camera in the cab that beeps if I yawn, and that's as much technology as I need in my life.
fieldNote: She sees her job as **secure** because of the union agreement and the supermarket's steady trade.
Her one live worry is **rent**, and she'd accept a longer early drive to cope.
She resents **cab monitoring** more than she fears automation.

steps.text: Keep the early supermarket store run and stay in the union
Put about a hundred a month into the savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the union branch meeting, that the bosses will use this to squeeze us, not to make the job better. The planning office shrinks, then they hand us tighter windows from a computer that's never seen a store yard. I'd be the one saying we need it written into the agreement before it comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the driving part of my job is probably safe for a while in that picture. It's the stuff around me that goes, the planners, the transport office girls who sort out problems when a store's shut. Then it's me ringing a chatbot at five in the morning when the shutter won't open, and that scares me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal on the new systems, no tracking-based discipline, no cutting the slack in the schedule. I'd keep driving, keep my head down, and put the savings up a bit, maybe a hundred and fifty a month. I'd skip the AI courses the company would offer, I'm not interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground under me hasn't moved yet, but I can hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, who's been there twenty years and knows every store manager by name. When a delivery goes wrong, Pat in the transport office sorts it in one phone call. Pat's job gets swallowed by a program and nobody notices until a snowstorm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip the AI courses. If the depot made one compulsory, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it and sit at the back. I'm not proud of being stubborn, but I've seen these courses before, they're about getting you to accept the thing, not about helping you. I'd learn just enough to not get written up.

say: I'd tell the branch meeting the bosses will use AI to **squeeze drivers**.
I'd say any new system must be **written into the agreement** first.
think: The **driving itself** looks safe for a while in this picture.
The office staff who fix problems, like **the planners**, go first and leave me alone.
do: Push the union for a **deal on tracking** and schedule slack within the year.
Raise savings to about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Do only the **compulsory AI training** and nothing more.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the ground hasn't moved yet but she can hear it.
S1.quote: When a delivery goes wrong, Pat in the transport office sorts it in one phone call. Pat's job gets swallowed by a program and nobody notices until a snowstorm.
fieldNote: Her fear is losing **human problem-solvers** around her, not losing the wheel.
She turns to the **union** before anything personal.
She admits her refusal to learn is **stubbornness**, but keeps it.

steps.text: Push the union branch for rules on cab tracking and schedules
Raise monthly savings to about a hundred and fifty
Keep driving the supermarket store runs as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, and fast. You can't let a handful of companies decide that every driver in the country is finished in five years. I'd be out on the march, if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm done as a driver by about 2031. In two years the planners and the office go, and three years after that the trucks drive themselves and unload themselves. I'd be thirty-one with a licence that's worth nothing and no idea what else I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to fight for redundancy terms and retraining money now, before the robots turn up. I'd stop spending on anything we don't need, no holiday, cancel the gym, and push every spare bit into savings. I'd keep driving every shift I can get while it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Really, it makes me feel sick, because I don't have a plan and I don't think I'm the kind of person who makes one quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes first and robots three years later. What does that gap mean for you in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three years of watching it coming with nothing to stop it. The office goes in 2028, so I'd be taking orders from a computer while I'm still driving, and then the computer gets hands. I suppose I'd use those three years to save hard, but save for what, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you realised that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop pretending the rent is the worst thing that can happen to us. His bus garage is in the same boat, buses will drive themselves too. I'd tell my partner Jonas we might both be out of work in the same year, and I'd want to know what his plan is, because I haven't got one.

say: I'd say the **government** must step in before companies finish every driver.
I'd join a **march** against it if one were organised.
think: She expects to be **finished as a driver** by about 2031.
At thirty-one she'd have a **worthless licence** and no clear other skill.
do: Push the union now for **redundancy terms** and retraining money.
Cut the **holiday and gym** and put every spare bit into savings.
Take **every shift** while driving work is still there.
feel: **Sick**, because she has no plan and doesn't think she'd make one quickly.
S2.quote: I'd tell my partner Jonas we might both be out of work in the same year, and I'd want to know what his plan is, because I haven't got one.
fieldNote: Both earners in the household, **driver and bus mechanic**, face the same robot date.
She treats the three-year gap as **time to save**, not to change.
Her resistance to change makes her **feel trapped** rather than angry.

steps.text: Press the union branch for redundancy and retraining money
Cancel the gym and skip this year's holiday
Put every spare pound from extra shifts into savings
Join marches calling for government limits on driverless trucks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say the government needs to set rules, but with five years there's a chance it actually happens. I'd be telling people at work to join the union now, not when the letters come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends the same way for me, just later. By 2031 the office side goes, by 2034 the trucks. I'd be thirty-four, and that's still young enough that people will say just retrain, like it's easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year getting the union to set up a proper fund for drivers. I'd probably ask about a forklift or warehouse certificate, something near the depot, because at least that's familiar. And I'd keep saving, two hundred a month if Jonas and I can manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sick than the fast one, but it would be on my mind every time I climbed into the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a warehouse certificate. Isn't the warehouse just as exposed to robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably more, you're right. I suppose I'm reaching for whatever's nearest, because the idea of going back to a classroom terrifies me. I left school with nothing special and I've never been good at sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would actually make retraining feel possible to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being paid while I do it, and doing it with people I know. If the union ran a retraining course at the depot for twenty of us, I'd go. On my own, at night, on a laptop, I'd never finish it.

say: I'd say five years gives the **government time** to set real rules.
I'd tell coworkers to **join the union** now, before the letters come.
think: The same end comes, just later, with the **office going in 2031**.
At thirty-four people will say **just retrain**, as if that were easy.
do: Get the union to set up a **drivers' fund** in the first year.
Ask about a **warehouse certificate** near the depot.
Save **two hundred a month** if the household budget allows.
feel: **Anxious**, less sick than before but present every time she climbs in.
S3.quote: If the union ran a retraining course at the depot for twenty of us, I'd go. On my own, at night, on a laptop, I'd never finish it.
fieldNote: She reaches for the **nearest familiar** option even when she knows it is exposed.
**Paid group training** through the union is the only route she believes in.
Her fear of the **classroom** is as strong as her fear of robots.

steps.text: Ask the union to start a fund and courses for drivers
Ask about a warehouse or forklift certificate near the depot
Save two hundred a month with her partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do it properly, with training paid for and nobody thrown on the scrapheap. I'd be on at the union rep to start planning now, not in nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels like forever and no time at all. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come. I'd probably drift for five years thinking it's far off, and that's what worries me about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, keep in the union, and maybe this time go for the extra licence for the bigger artic trucks, because that work would last longest. I'd ask Jonas to look at what he could do with his mechanic skills, because someone has to fix the robots. And I'd keep saving, steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, and then anxious when I think about how I'd waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might drift. What would stop you drifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date on the wall, honestly. If the union said by 2030 every driver gets a training place, I'd turn up. I'm good at turning up, I'm bad at starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself at thirty-seven in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe still at the depot doing something, checking the trucks, sorting the cages. I can't picture a version of me in an office, and in this picture the office is gone anyway.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it **properly and fairly**.
I'd push the **union rep** to start planning now, not later.
think: She'd be **thirty-seven** when the robots arrive.
She fears she'd **drift for years** thinking the change is far away.
do: Keep driving and stay **in the union**.
Get the **artic licence** for the bigger trucks that would last longest.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then **anxious** about wasting the decade.
S4.quote: If the union said by 2030 every driver gets a training place, I'd turn up. I'm good at turning up, I'm bad at starting.
fieldNote: She knows her **weakness is starting**, not effort.
She hopes her partner's **mechanic skills** could carry the household.
Even with a decade she **can't picture** a new career for herself.

steps.text: Keep driving the supermarket runs while the work lasts
Book the test for the bigger articulated truck licence
Push the union rep to set a date for training places
Keep a fixed monthly transfer into savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, definitely, AGI by 2028. What would help is the government and the union having a plan before it lands, paid training with people I know, and some guarantee on rent so we don't lose the flat while we work it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't good with change. Everyone talks about retraining like it's a light switch, but some of us need someone to walk us through the door. I'd do the work, I just can't find the door on my own.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about retraining like it's a light switch, but some of us need someone to walk us through the door.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** supermarket depot driver who rents a flat with her partner, a bus mechanic.
She trusts the **union** and wants government rules before any technology changes her job.
She avoids **AI tools** and resents the cab camera more than she fears robots today.
She moves from **calm** in the hype picture to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
She knows she is **slow to start** change and needs paid, group training to move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and her partner could lose work in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: A **government plan**, union-run group training and **rent protection** while she adjusts.
